titre: Tokyo (1946–1948): The Judge Who Refused the Verdict
accroche: In 1948, Tokyo tries twenty-five Japanese leaders. Only one of the eleven judges rejects the verdict and writes, alone, more than a thousand pages to acquit them.
contenu_vulgarise:
On November 12, 1948, in Tokyo, eleven judges from eleven countries finish reading a judgment begun eight days earlier. Twenty-five Japanese defendants learn their fate: seven will be hanged, sixteen will spend the rest of their lives in prison. One of the eleven judges signed nothing in this collective text. The Indian judge Radhabinod Pal wrote, on his own, more than a thousand pages concluding that all the defendants should be acquitted.

## Twenty-Eight Defendants, Eleven Judges

The tribunal is created on January 19, 1946 by a proclamation of General Douglas MacArthur, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, who attaches to it the same day a charter modeled on that of the Nuremberg tribunal. Eleven judges sit on it, one for each country represented: Australia, Canada, China, the United States, France, India, New Zealand, the Netherlands, the Philippines, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union. Twenty-eight Japanese leaders are indicted for crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity. The trial opens on April 29, 1946. Two defendants die during the proceedings, a third is ruled unfit: only twenty-five men hear the verdict. Seven are sentenced to death, including former prime minister Hideki Tojo. General MacArthur confirms the sentence on November 24, and the hangings take place on December 23, 1948 at Sugamo Prison. Sixteen defendants receive life in prison, and two others sentences of seven and twenty years.

One name is missing from this list: Emperor Hirohito. Neither he nor any member of the imperial family is prosecuted, or even called to testify. The American occupation authorities judge that they need him to keep order in Japan, and several defendants quietly shape their testimony so as not to implicate him. This choice remains an occupation decision, made before the trial, not an argument debated before the tribunal.

## Pal, Alone Against Ten

Judge Pal starts from a simple principle: a law cannot punish an act committed before it existed. Yet the charge of "crime against peace," which weighs on most of the defendants, was written in no text before the 1946 charter itself. Pal does not deny the atrocities committed in Asia; he even accepts that ordinary war crimes fall within the tribunal's jurisdiction. But he refuses to judge as criminal, after the fact, a war of aggression that nothing defined as such at the time it was waged. On this basis, he votes to acquit all the defendants on all counts.

His opinion, titled "Dissentient Judgment of Mr. Justice Pal," is first kept out of publication by the occupation authorities. The tribunal's translation service, in making it known in Japan, drops the word "dissentient": the text circulates there under the name "Pal Judgment" alone, as if it had the same authority as the majority judgment it opposes.

## What This Shifts

Nuremberg had established individual criminal responsibility as a principle. Tokyo shows what happens when that principle is applied to a war that no one had defined as a crime before it was lost. The question Pal raises is not about the cruelty of the facts, which he does not dispute, but about the moment when a prohibition begins to exist.

repere.texte: Of twenty-eight defendants, two die during the trial and one is ruled unfit: twenty-five are tried. Seven are sentenced to death and hanged on December 23, 1948, sixteen to life in prison. Only one of the eleven judges, Radhabinod Pal (India), votes to acquit all of them.
repere.source: Wikipedia (contributors), “International Military Tribunal for the Far East”

carte.punch: Eleven judges try Tokyo in 1948. One writes a thousand pages alone to acquit everyone.
carte.idee: In 1948, the Tokyo tribunal sentences seven Japanese leaders to death and sixteen to life in prison. Only one of the eleven judges, India's Radhabinod Pal, rejects the verdict: he finds it impossible to punish after the fact a war that nothing defined as a crime when it took place.

quiz.question: Why does Judge Pal vote to acquit all the defendants in Tokyo?
choix: He finds that the evidence is lacking against most of the defendants
He believes that only the emperor bore responsibility, not his ministers
He refuses to punish as a crime a war that no text defined as such before the 1946 charter
He holds that an international tribunal has no jurisdiction over acts committed in Asia
quiz.explication: Pal accepts the tribunal's jurisdiction over ordinary war crimes and does not doubt the evidence: he rejects only the charge of crime against peace, absent from any text before the charter that created the tribunal.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who confirms the Tokyo tribunal's sentence, and on what date?
choix: The tribunal itself, on November 12, 1948, the day the judgment was read
Judge Pal, on December 23, 1948, the day of the hangings
General MacArthur, on December 23, 1948, the day of the hangings
General MacArthur, on November 24, 1948, before the hangings
quiz_supplementaire.explication: General MacArthur confirms the sentence on November 24, 1948. The hangings do not take place until a month later, on December 23, at Sugamo Prison.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why is Emperor Hirohito neither prosecuted nor called to testify?
choix: The tribunal, after an adversarial debate among the judges
The American occupation authorities, to keep order in Japan
The defendants themselves, who asked that he be implicated
General MacArthur, who had indicted him as early as January 1946
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The decision came from the occupation authorities, made before the trial. It was not debated before the tribunal, and the judges did not rule on it.
